summary: Defines MIB textual conventions for representing network layer addresses. It was replaced by RFC 4001.

eli5.summary: Instead of every MIB inventing its own way to write addresses, this offers shared ones. It has been replaced by RFC 4001.

questions: what are inet address textual conventions
how do mib modules represent ipv6 addresses
how do zone indices work in ipv6 addresses
subtitle: Standard definitions for how MIBs represent Internet addresses and related values.

tldr.problem: SNMP MIBs use the IpAddress base type, which only handles IPv4 addresses. With IPv6 becoming common, MIB designers had no standard way to represent addresses that work across IP versions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3291 defines textual conventions (reusable data type definitions) for representing Internet addresses and related values in MIBs, supporting IPv4, IPv6, and DNS names with flexibility for future address types.
tldr.outcome: MIB modules can now support multiple address types uniformly without reinventing the wheel. The specification was later refined in RFC 4001.

today: RFC 3291 is a Standards Track specification. It was superseded by RFC 4001, which provides additional clarifications and refinements based on deployment experience with IPv6 management.

sections.title: The IPv4-Only Problem
sections.content:
SNMP MIBs use the IpAddress base type to represent network addresses. However, IpAddress only holds IPv4 addresses (4 bytes). When IPv6 became essential, MIB designers faced a dilemma: they either had to create separate, parallel MIB definitions for IPv6, or invent their own proprietary ways to handle it. Both approaches are messy and hard to maintain.

RFC 3291 solves this by defining standardized textual conventions that represent addresses in a flexible way. A MIB designer can import these definitions and use them to support IPv4, IPv6, DNS names, and any future address format the community might invent, all in a single, unified MIB module.
sections.eli5: Network management tools used to only understand IPv4 addresses. When IPv6 came along, people had to write confusing workarounds. These conventions let tools handle both kinds of addresses the same way.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and the Type Pair
sections.content:
A textual convention (TC) is a reusable data type in SNMP. This RFC defines a small set of TCs that work together as a unit. The foundation is an InetAddressType enumeration that says what kind of address follows, plus an InetAddress object that holds the actual address bytes. This type pair pattern allows a MIB to handle any address format by checking the type first.

For example, if an InetAddressType field has value ipv4(1), the corresponding InetAddress holds 4 bytes; if it says ipv6(2), the same field can hold 16 bytes. If it says dns(16), it holds a text string. This design is forward-compatible: new address types can be added to the type enumeration without changing existing MIB modules.
sections.eli5: Think of InetAddressType as a label that says what kind of address follows. It acts like a translator, so the same container (InetAddress) can hold IPv4, IPv6, or even a domain name.

sections.title: Address Types and Conventions
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven address types. InetAddressIPv4 represents a 4-byte IPv4 address like 192.0.2.1. InetAddressIPv6 represents a 16-byte global IPv6 address. InetAddressIPv4z and InetAddressIPv6z are variants for non-global (scoped) addresses, each paired with a zone index to disambiguate identical addresses on different interfaces. InetAddressDNS holds a fully-qualified domain name as text.

The RFC also defines InetAddressPrefixLength (how many bits in a network prefix), InetPortNumber (a 16-bit transport-layer port from 0 to 65535), and InetAutonomousSystemNumber (an AS number, now 32-bit to support the expanded AS space). Together, these cover the most common network layer and transport layer values MIBs need to represent.
sections.eli5: There are several types: regular IPv4, regular IPv6, IPv4 with a zone marker, IPv6 with a zone marker, or a domain name. Plus port numbers and AS numbers. MIBs can pick which ones they support.

sections.title: Using These in MIBs
sections.content:
When a MIB module defines a table that includes network addresses, it imports the textual conventions and creates two columns: one with type InetAddressType (the index) and one with type InetAddress (the data). The type column must come first in the table's sort order, so tools can interpret the address column correctly. The MIB author describes in the DESCRIPTION clause how the address field should be used.

For example, a table of management peers might include an index like (peerAddressType, peerAddress). An SNMP client can then look up a peer by specifying both the type (say, ipv6) and the address value. This same table automatically works for IPv4 peers, IPv6 peers, or DNS-name peers without any code change needed; the implementation just respects whichever type is in use.
sections.eli5: MIB writers use these conventions to build tables. The type field says which address format is being used, and the address field holds the actual data. This way, one table can handle IPv4, IPv6, or domain names.

sections.title: Zone Indices and IPv6 Scoping
sections.content:
IPv6 addresses have scopes: global (unicast), link-local (usable only on a single link), and site-local (usable within a site). A link-local address like fe80::1 can appear on many interfaces at once and is only unique within that link. To specify which interface is meant, IPv6 uses a zone index (also called a scope id).

The InetAddressIPv6z convention includes both the 16-byte IPv6 address and a 4-byte zone index, making the combination globally unique on that node. Similarly, InetAddressIPv4z supports IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses with zone indices. MIB writers who need to track non-global addresses across multiple zones should use these 'z' variants; writers whose devices only have single interfaces or only track global addresses can use the simpler InetAddressIPv6 type.
sections.eli5: IPv6 addresses can be local to one cable or one building. To say which cable or building you mean, you add a zone number. These conventions handle that automatically.
